glossary.text: The federal agency that runs Medicare, oversees Medicaid and the Marketplaces, and writes many of the rules health plans follow. Its audits and final rules drive much of the regulatory library here.

glossary.full: Department of Health and Human Services
glossary.text: The federal department that includes CMS and the Office for Civil Rights. It issues the HIPAA rules and many health plan regulations.
The part of HHS that enforces HIPAA and the substance use disorder records rule. Breaches affecting 500 or more people are reported to it.
The HHS watchdog that investigates fraud and keeps the list of people and companies excluded from federal health programs. Its guidance describes what an effective compliance program looks like.
The state agency that licenses insurers and enforces state insurance law, including prompt payment and data security rules. Each state where a plan is licensed has its own.
The body through which state insurance regulators write model laws. States adopt those models, often with changes, so the enacted version in each state is what counts.
Medicare coverage delivered by private health plans under contract with CMS, also called Part C. These plans face CMS program audits and specific decision timeframes.
A plan certified to be sold on a health insurance Marketplace under the Affordable Care Act. It must meet federal benefit, network and transparency standards.

The 2010 federal law that set market rules for health insurance, such as appeal rights, the Summary of Benefits and Coverage and the medical loss ratio. Many obligations in the library come from its regulations.
The federal law that governs employer-sponsored benefit plans. Its claims procedure regulation sets time limits for deciding claims and appeals in group health plans.

glossary.full: Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act
glossary.text: The federal law requiring that limits on mental health and substance use disorder benefits are no stricter than those on medical benefits. Plans must document a comparative analysis to show it.
A limit on care that is not a number, such as prior authorization or network admission standards. Parity law requires these to be applied no more strictly to mental health benefits.
The federal law that protects members from surprise bills for emergency and certain out-of-network care. It sets payment deadlines and a dispute process between plans and providers.
The federal process that settles payment disputes between a plan and an out-of-network provider under the No Surprises Act. A certified third party picks one side's offer.
The share of premium a plan spends on claims and quality improvement. Plans that fall below 80 or 85 percent, depending on the market, owe rebates.
A standard short document that describes what a plan covers and what it costs. Federal rules set its format and when members must receive it.
The statement a plan sends after processing a claim, showing what was billed, what the plan paid and what the member owes. A denial on it must explain the reason and appeal rights.
The plan's review of whether care is covered and medically necessary, including prior authorization and concurrent review. Regulations set how quickly each decision must be made.
The plan's approval, requested before care is given, that a service will be covered. Federal rules set decision deadlines, such as 72 hours for expedited requests in Medicare Advantage.
A review during an ongoing course of treatment, such as a hospital stay, to approve more days or services. Urgent requests have short decision deadlines.
A claim that arrives with everything needed to process it, with no missing information. Prompt payment laws start their clock when a clean claim is received.
A denial, reduction or termination of a benefit, in whole or in part. It triggers the member's right to appeal and, in many cases, to external review.
A member's or provider's request that the plan reconsider a denial. Regulations set how fast it must be decided and what the decision notice must say.
A complaint about the plan or its providers that is not about a coverage denial, such as service quality or wait times. Regulations set timelines for resolving it.
An outside organization that reviews a plan's denial after the plan's own appeal upholds it. In commercial coverage the same role is played by an independent review organization.

glossary.full: First Tier, Downstream and Related Entity
glossary.text: CMS's term for a company a Medicare plan pays to do part of its work, and that company's own subcontractors. The plan stays accountable for everything they do.

A company the plan has handed a function to, such as utilization management, claims processing or pharmacy benefits. The plan must check its performance and controls before and during the arrangement.
A company that processes claims and runs benefits for a plan or an employer. It is treated as a delegate here, so its service levels and assessments are tracked.
A company that runs the prescription drug benefit for a plan, including the drug list and pharmacy network. It is treated as a delegate here.
Checking a provider's license, training and history before they join the plan's network, and again at set intervals. It is tracked on each provider's record.
Billing or behavior that takes money from a health program improperly, whether by intent or carelessness. Plans must detect it, investigate it and report it.
The team inside a plan that investigates suspected fraud. Fraud alerts raised here are leads for that team, not conclusions.

glossary.full: List of Excluded Individuals and Entities
glossary.text: The OIG's list of people and companies barred from federal health programs. Plans screen staff, providers and delegates against it, usually monthly.
The CMS system in which insurers register plans and file data. The plan identifier it issues is recorded on each product.
The time taken to finish a step, such as deciding a prior authorization request or paying a claim. Timeline rules compare each case's turnaround time with the limit that applies.
The service standards a vendor has agreed to in its contract, such as decision time or call answer rate. Performance against each one is tracked and misses are flagged.
Setting the terms and price on which a group or person is covered, within what the law allows. Exceptions to the filed rules need a recorded approval.

The combined practice of directing an organization, managing what could go wrong, and proving that laws and rules are followed. This platform keeps all three in one place so they can be traced to each other.
The action taken to fix a problem that was found, and to stop it happening again. Each one is tracked to completion and then verified as effective by someone independent.
A measure of how well something is working, such as the share of prior authorization requests decided within the limit. Each one here shows its calculation rule.
An early-warning measure showing that a risk is becoming more likely, such as rising claim denials. It turns amber or red when it crosses the thresholds you set.
A traffic-light status. Red needs action now, amber needs attention, and green is within limits.
Splitting a task so that no single person can both carry it out and approve it. For example, the person who raises a corrective action cannot verify it.
The senior person accountable for the organization meeting its legal and regulatory duties. In this platform the role approves obligations and compliance conclusions.
The senior person accountable for identifying and managing the organization's risks. In this platform the role approves risk assessments and risk acceptance.
The senior person accountable for protecting systems and data. Information security registers and incidents are overseen by this role.
A named set of rules or standards the organization follows, such as the HIPAA Security Rule or NIST CSF. Obligations and control mappings are grouped under it.
One numbered provision inside a regulation or standard. Obligations point back to the exact clause they come from.
One specific thing the organization must do or not do because a law, regulation or contract says so. It counts towards compliance figures only after a compliance officer approves it.
Whether an obligation applies to this organization, given its licenses, products and activities. Obligations marked not applicable are excluded from the figures, with the reason recorded.
A safeguard that reduces a risk or helps meet an obligation, such as a second approval or an access review. Controls are tested to show that they work.
A document or data set that proves a control was carried out. It is reviewed by a person before it is accepted, and it expires.
A confirmed weakness or breach identified by an audit, a test or a check. It stays open until corrective action is completed and closure is approved.
The size of a risk before any controls are considered. It is scored as likelihood multiplied by impact, out of 25.
The risk that remains after the controls in place are taken into account. This is the figure compared with the risk appetite.
The amount of risk the organization is willing to accept. A residual risk above this level needs treatment or a formally approved acceptance.
A grid that plots risks by likelihood and impact. Risks in the darker cells towards the top right need attention first.
Being able to follow one requirement from the regulation through to the control, evidence, test, finding and fix. It is what an auditor or regulator asks to see.
An auditor's record of the procedure performed, what was examined and the result. Workpapers support the conclusions in the audit report.
Matching two sets of records, such as claims paid against bank payments, to find and explain differences. Unexplained differences are followed up.
Testing a selected portion of records instead of every one, and drawing a conclusion about the whole. The selection method and seed are recorded so the sample can be reproduced.

glossary.full: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
glossary.text: The federal law that protects health information. Its Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules apply to health plans and to the vendors that handle their data.
Health information that can be tied to a person and is held by a plan, a provider or their vendors. HIPAA limits how it is used and shared; ePHI is the electronic form.
The contract HIPAA requires before a vendor handles protected health information for a plan. It sets permitted uses, safeguards and breach reporting duties.
The document that tells members how the plan uses their health information and what rights they have. HIPAA sets its content and when it must be given.
The federal rule that gives extra protection to substance use disorder treatment records. It limits disclosure beyond what HIPAA alone requires.
A certifiable security framework widely used in United States health care. Business partners often ask for it as proof of security controls.
Information that can identify a person, such as a name, phone number or member ID. Fields holding it are marked, masked in exports and never sent to an AI model by default.
Signing in with two proofs of identity: a password and a code from an authenticator app on your phone. A stolen password alone is then not enough to get in.
Signing in through your organization's own identity system, such as Microsoft Entra ID, Google or Okta. People use one account, and access ends when that account is disabled.
The open standard this platform uses for single sign-on. It lets your identity provider confirm who a person is without sharing their password.
The six-digit code an authenticator app shows, which changes every 30 seconds. It is the second step when multi-factor authentication is on.

An impermissible use or disclosure of protected health information that compromises its security or privacy. Unless a risk assessment shows a low probability of compromise, affected people and HHS must be notified.
The plan for keeping essential services running during a disruption. It is tested periodically and the results are recorded.
Restoring systems and data after a serious failure. Tests measure how quickly service returns and how much data could be lost.
The longest time a system may be unavailable after a failure. A disaster recovery test checks whether this target was met.
The greatest amount of recent data, measured in time, that may be lost in a failure. It determines how often backups must run.

glossary.full: International standard for information security management
glossary.text: A widely used standard describing how to manage information security systematically. Controls here can be mapped to its requirements.
An independent audit report on a service provider's security, availability and confidentiality controls. Health plans often ask vendors for one.

glossary.full: National Institute of Standards and Technology Cybersecurity Framework
glossary.text: A voluntary framework that organizes cyber security work into govern, identify, protect, detect, respond and recover. It is offered here as an optional mapping.
The encrypted way a browser talks to a website. It stops others on the network reading or altering what is sent.
Software that drafts, summarizes or flags items for a person to review. Here it only recommends: approvals and compliance conclusions are always made by people.
A defined way for one computer system to send data to or request data from another. Other systems feed claims and evidence into this platform through it.
Reading the text out of a scanned page or image so it can be searched and analyzed. It is used for bulletins and letters that arrive as scanned documents.
A standard format for exchanging health care data between systems. The CMS interoperability rules require plans to offer FHIR-based APIs, including one for prior authorization.
A simple spreadsheet file format that almost every system can read and write. Registers can be imported from and exported to it.
A message one system sends to another the moment something happens. Workflows can be started by one, or can send one to tools such as Slack or Teams.
A sequence of automatic steps, such as creating a task, asking for approval and sending a reminder, started by an event. People still make the decisions inside it.
A small read-only program that gathers proof from another system, such as who has administrator access. It sends the result here as evidence for a control.
An automation tool that connects systems through visual workflows. Ready-made n8n workflows are supplied for collecting evidence and sending alerts.
The system that holds employee records. It can supply joiner and leaver data for access reviews and training.
A system that collects security logs and raises alerts on suspicious activity. Its alerts can be fed in as security incidents.
The tool used to log and track IT requests, incidents and changes, such as Jira or ServiceNow. Tickets can be collected as evidence of a control operating.
The system that records customer contacts and service requests. Grievances can be fed from it.
The finance and operations system of record. It can supply data for financial reconciliations.

agents.name: Regulatory Intelligence Agent
agents.does: Reads a regulatory document and proposes clauses and obligations for the compliance team to validate.

agents.name: Compliance Mapping Agent
agents.does: Recommends which existing controls address an obligation, or drafts a new control where there is a gap.

agents.name: Risk Assessment Agent
agents.does: Suggests likelihood, impact and control effectiveness from linked controls, tests, findings and KRIs.

agents.name: Evidence Validation Agent
agents.does: Checks evidence for completeness, relevance, validity dates and inconsistencies before a reviewer decides.

agents.name: Claims Audit Agent
agents.does: Looks across claims and exceptions for unusual patterns by delegate, hospital, override and rejection reason.

agents.name: Third-Party Risk Agent
agents.does: Summarizes a delegate, hospital or vendor's weak areas from assessments, SLAs and incidents, with follow-up actions.

agents.name: Audit Reporting Agent
agents.does: Drafts the audit report from recorded findings, and suggests root cause lines of enquiry for a finding.

clause.title: Human oversight of AI
clause.text: AI outputs that inform coverage or compliance conclusions are reviewed by an authorized person and the review is recorded.

clause.title: Access control
clause.text: Asset owners review access rights regularly and remove access that is no longer needed.

clause.title: Asset management
clause.text: Identify information assets, assign owners and classify them by sensitivity.

clause.title: Utilization management
clause.text: Make utilization management decisions and send notices within the accreditation timeframes, with the required content in each denial notice.

clause.title: Reporting line
clause.text: Keep an anonymous or confidential reporting channel, publicize it, and enforce a non-retaliation policy.

clause.title: Notice to HHS and the media
clause.text: For a breach affecting 500 or more people, notify HHS within 60 calendar days of discovery, and prominent media when more than 500 residents of one state are affected. Report smaller breaches to HHS within 60 days after the end of the calendar year.

clause.title: Notice to individuals
clause.text: After a breach of unsecured protected health information, notify each affected person without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after discovery.

clause.title: Security incident procedures
clause.text: Have procedures to detect and respond to suspected or known security incidents, reduce their harm and record the outcome.

clause.title: Security awareness and training
clause.text: Run a security awareness and training program for all workforce members, including management.

clause.title: Contingency plan
clause.text: Keep retrievable copies of health information, a plan to restore lost data and a plan to keep critical processes running, and test them.

clause.title: Audit controls and activity review
clause.text: Keep audit logs for systems with electronic protected health information and review them on a regular schedule.

clause.title: Access controls
clause.text: Give each user a unique identity, grant access by role, and review and remove access that is no longer needed.

clause.title: Risk analysis and risk management
clause.text: Assess the risks and vulnerabilities to electronic protected health information across all systems that hold it, and apply security measures that reduce those risks to a reasonable level.

clause.title: Business associates
clause.text: Have a written agreement with each business associate that sets permitted uses, safeguards and breach reporting duties.

clause.title: Minimum necessary
clause.text: Give each role only the health information it needs, and limit routine disclosures and requests in the same way.

clause.title: Right of access
clause.text: Respond to an access request within 30 calendar days. The Privacy Rule changes issued November 16, 2026 shorten this to 15 calendar days once their compliance date arrives.

clause.title: Notice of Privacy Practices
clause.text: Provide the notice at enrollment, post it on the website, and tell members at least every three years that it is available. Update it when privacy practices or the rules change.

clause.title: Machine-readable files and price tool
clause.text: Post in-network negotiated rates and out-of-network allowed amounts as public machine-readable files updated monthly, and give members an online tool with personalized cost estimates.

clause.title: Comparative analysis

regulatory_change.impact_assessment: Access request procedure, fee schedule page and notice wording need updating. One control to be redesigned.

items.report:
DRAFT AUDIT REPORT: Claims operations audit 2026 (AUD-0001)

1. Scope and objectives
Prior authorization and post-service claims processed in the last two quarters.
Assess turnaround compliance, denial controls and approval authority.

2. Work performed
4 of 4 planned procedures completed. 2 resulted in observations.

3. Summary of findings
2 high, 1 medium, 1 low

4. Detailed findings
4.1 Approval authority overridden without recorded justification [High] (FND-0009) [S3]
   Observation: Three approvals above L1 limit by L1 users.
   Root cause: Authority matrix not enforced for manual override path.
   Status: CAPA in progress

4.2 Expedited prior authorization decisions exceeded 72 hours in 13% of sampled cases [High] (FND-0007) [S5]
   Observation: Sample of 60 requests; 8 exceeded the limit without a documented reason.
   Root cause: No weekend coverage at the center; no automated queue alert.
   Status: CAPA in progress

4.3 Denial notices did not give a specific reason in 5 of 30 samples [Medium] (FND-0008) [S4]
   Observation: Reason given in general terms only.
   Root cause: Template allows free text without a reason code.
   Status: Pending verification

4.4 Concurrent review escalation log incomplete [Low] (FND-0012) [S2]
   Observation: Escalations not logged for weekend shifts.
   Root cause: Weekend roster missed in procedure.
   Status: Closed

5. Management actions
Corrective and preventive actions are tracked in the CAPA register against each finding.

This draft was generated for auditor review. It contains no audit opinion; conclusions are the auditor's.

glossary.text: The federal agency that runs Medicare, oversees Medicaid and the Marketplaces, and writes many of the rules health plans follow. Its audits and final rules drive much of the regulatory library here.

glossary.full: Department of Health and Human Services
glossary.text: The federal department that includes CMS and the Office for Civil Rights. It issues the HIPAA rules and many health plan regulations.
The part of HHS that enforces HIPAA and the substance use disorder records rule. Breaches affecting 500 or more people are reported to it.
The HHS watchdog that investigates fraud and keeps the list of people and companies excluded from federal health programs. Its guidance describes what an effective compliance program looks like.
The state agency that licenses insurers and enforces state insurance law, including prompt payment and data security rules. Each state where a plan is licensed has its own.
The body through which state insurance regulators write model laws. States adopt those models, often with changes, so the enacted version in each state is what counts.
Medicare coverage delivered by private health plans under contract with CMS, also called Part C. These plans face CMS program audits and specific decision timeframes.
A plan certified to be sold on a health insurance Marketplace under the Affordable Care Act. It must meet federal benefit, network and transparency standards.

The 2010 federal law that set market rules for health insurance, such as appeal rights, the Summary of Benefits and Coverage and the medical loss ratio. Many obligations in the library come from its regulations.
The federal law that governs employer-sponsored benefit plans. Its claims procedure regulation sets time limits for deciding claims and appeals in group health plans.

glossary.full: Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act
glossary.text: The federal law requiring that limits on mental health and substance use disorder benefits are no stricter than those on medical benefits. Plans must document a comparative analysis to show it.
A limit on care that is not a number, such as prior authorization or network admission standards. Parity law requires these to be applied no more strictly to mental health benefits.
The federal law that protects members from surprise bills for emergency and certain out-of-network care. It sets payment deadlines and a dispute process between plans and providers.
The federal process that settles payment disputes between a plan and an out-of-network provider under the No Surprises Act. A certified third party picks one side's offer.
The share of premium a plan spends on claims and quality improvement. Plans that fall below 80 or 85 percent, depending on the market, owe rebates.
A standard short document that describes what a plan covers and what it costs. Federal rules set its format and when members must receive it.
The statement a plan sends after processing a claim, showing what was billed, what the plan paid and what the member owes. A denial on it must explain the reason and appeal rights.
The plan's review of whether care is covered and medically necessary, including prior authorization and concurrent review. Regulations set how quickly each decision must be made.
The plan's approval, requested before care is given, that a service will be covered. Federal rules set decision deadlines, such as 72 hours for expedited requests in Medicare Advantage.
A review during an ongoing course of treatment, such as a hospital stay, to approve more days or services. Urgent requests have short decision deadlines.
A claim that arrives with everything needed to process it, with no missing information. Prompt payment laws start their clock when a clean claim is received.
A denial, reduction or termination of a benefit, in whole or in part. It triggers the member's right to appeal and, in many cases, to external review.
A member's or provider's request that the plan reconsider a denial. Regulations set how fast it must be decided and what the decision notice must say.
A complaint about the plan or its providers that is not about a coverage denial, such as service quality or wait times. Regulations set timelines for resolving it.
An outside organization that reviews a plan's denial after the plan's own appeal upholds it. In commercial coverage the same role is played by an independent review organization.

glossary.full: First Tier, Downstream and Related Entity
glossary.text: CMS's term for a company a Medicare plan pays to do part of its work, and that company's own subcontractors. The plan stays accountable for everything they do.

A company the plan has handed a function to, such as utilization management, claims processing or pharmacy benefits. The plan must check its performance and controls before and during the arrangement.
A company that processes claims and runs benefits for a plan or an employer. It is treated as a delegate here, so its service levels and assessments are tracked.
A company that runs the prescription drug benefit for a plan, including the drug list and pharmacy network. It is treated as a delegate here.
Checking a provider's license, training and history before they join the plan's network, and again at set intervals. It is tracked on each provider's record.
Billing or behavior that takes money from a health program improperly, whether by intent or carelessness. Plans must detect it, investigate it and report it.
The team inside a plan that investigates suspected fraud. Fraud alerts raised here are leads for that team, not conclusions.

glossary.full: List of Excluded Individuals and Entities
glossary.text: The OIG's list of people and companies barred from federal health programs. Plans screen staff, providers and delegates against it, usually monthly.
The CMS system in which insurers register plans and file data. The plan identifier it issues is recorded on each product.
The time taken to finish a step, such as deciding a prior authorization request or paying a claim. Timeline rules compare each case's turnaround time with the limit that applies.
The service standards a vendor has agreed to in its contract, such as decision time or call answer rate. Performance against each one is tracked and misses are flagged.
Setting the terms and price on which a group or person is covered, within what the law allows. Exceptions to the filed rules need a recorded approval.

The combined practice of directing an organization, managing what could go wrong, and proving that laws and rules are followed. This platform keeps all three in one place so they can be traced to each other.
The action taken to fix a problem that was found, and to stop it happening again. Each one is tracked to completion and then verified as effective by someone independent.
A measure of how well something is working, such as the share of prior authorization requests decided within the limit. Each one here shows its calculation rule.
An early-warning measure showing that a risk is becoming more likely, such as rising claim denials. It turns amber or red when it crosses the thresholds you set.
A traffic-light status. Red needs action now, amber needs attention, and green is within limits.
Splitting a task so that no single person can both carry it out and approve it. For example, the person who raises a corrective action cannot verify it.
The senior person accountable for the organization meeting its legal and regulatory duties. In this platform the role approves obligations and compliance conclusions.
The senior person accountable for identifying and managing the organization's risks. In this platform the role approves risk assessments and risk acceptance.
The senior person accountable for protecting systems and data. Information security registers and incidents are overseen by this role.
A named set of rules or standards the organization follows, such as the HIPAA Security Rule or NIST CSF. Obligations and control mappings are grouped under it.
One numbered provision inside a regulation or standard. Obligations point back to the exact clause they come from.
One specific thing the organization must do or not do because a law, regulation or contract says so. It counts towards compliance figures only after a compliance officer approves it.
Whether an obligation applies to this organization, given its licenses, products and activities. Obligations marked not applicable are excluded from the figures, with the reason recorded.
A safeguard that reduces a risk or helps meet an obligation, such as a second approval or an access review. Controls are tested to show that they work.
A document or data set that proves a control was carried out. It is reviewed by a person before it is accepted, and it expires.
A confirmed weakness or breach identified by an audit, a test or a check. It stays open until corrective action is completed and closure is approved.
The size of a risk before any controls are considered. It is scored as likelihood multiplied by impact, out of 25.
The risk that remains after the controls in place are taken into account. This is the figure compared with the risk appetite.
The amount of risk the organization is willing to accept. A residual risk above this level needs treatment or a formally approved acceptance.
A grid that plots risks by likelihood and impact. Risks in the darker cells towards the top right need attention first.
Being able to follow one requirement from the regulation through to the control, evidence, test, finding and fix. It is what an auditor or regulator asks to see.
An auditor's record of the procedure performed, what was examined and the result. Workpapers support the conclusions in the audit report.
Matching two sets of records, such as claims paid against bank payments, to find and explain differences. Unexplained differences are followed up.
Testing a selected portion of records instead of every one, and drawing a conclusion about the whole. The selection method and seed are recorded so the sample can be reproduced.

glossary.full: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
glossary.text: The federal law that protects health information. Its Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules apply to health plans and to the vendors that handle their data.
Health information that can be tied to a person and is held by a plan, a provider or their vendors. HIPAA limits how it is used and shared; ePHI is the electronic form.
The contract HIPAA requires before a vendor handles protected health information for a plan. It sets permitted uses, safeguards and breach reporting duties.
The document that tells members how the plan uses their health information and what rights they have. HIPAA sets its content and when it must be given.
The federal rule that gives extra protection to substance use disorder treatment records. It limits disclosure beyond what HIPAA alone requires.
A certifiable security framework widely used in United States health care. Business partners often ask for it as proof of security controls.
Information that can identify a person, such as a name, phone number or member ID. Fields holding it are marked, masked in exports and never sent to an AI model by default.
Signing in with two proofs of identity: a password and a code from an authenticator app on your phone. A stolen password alone is then not enough to get in.
Signing in through your organization's own identity system, such as Microsoft Entra ID, Google or Okta. People use one account, and access ends when that account is disabled.
The open standard this platform uses for single sign-on. It lets your identity provider confirm who a person is without sharing their password.
The six-digit code an authenticator app shows, which changes every 30 seconds. It is the second step when multi-factor authentication is on.

An impermissible use or disclosure of protected health information that compromises its security or privacy. Unless a risk assessment shows a low probability of compromise, affected people and HHS must be notified.
The plan for keeping essential services running during a disruption. It is tested periodically and the results are recorded.
Restoring systems and data after a serious failure. Tests measure how quickly service returns and how much data could be lost.
The longest time a system may be unavailable after a failure. A disaster recovery test checks whether this target was met.
The greatest amount of recent data, measured in time, that may be lost in a failure. It determines how often backups must run.

glossary.full: International standard for information security management
glossary.text: A widely used standard describing how to manage information security systematically. Controls here can be mapped to its requirements.
An independent audit report on a service provider's security, availability and confidentiality controls. Health plans often ask vendors for one.

glossary.full: National Institute of Standards and Technology Cybersecurity Framework
glossary.text: A voluntary framework that organizes cyber security work into govern, identify, protect, detect, respond and recover. It is offered here as an optional mapping.
The encrypted way a browser talks to a website. It stops others on the network reading or altering what is sent.
Software that drafts, summarizes or flags items for a person to review. Here it only recommends: approvals and compliance conclusions are always made by people.
A defined way for one computer system to send data to or request data from another. Other systems feed claims and evidence into this platform through it.
Reading the text out of a scanned page or image so it can be searched and analyzed. It is used for bulletins and letters that arrive as scanned documents.
A standard format for exchanging health care data between systems. The CMS interoperability rules require plans to offer FHIR-based APIs, including one for prior authorization.
A simple spreadsheet file format that almost every system can read and write. Registers can be imported from and exported to it.
A message one system sends to another the moment something happens. Workflows can be started by one, or can send one to tools such as Slack or Teams.
A sequence of automatic steps, such as creating a task, asking for approval and sending a reminder, started by an event. People still make the decisions inside it.
A small read-only program that gathers proof from another system, such as who has administrator access. It sends the result here as evidence for a control.
An automation tool that connects systems through visual workflows. Ready-made n8n workflows are supplied for collecting evidence and sending alerts.
The system that holds employee records. It can supply joiner and leaver data for access reviews and training.
A system that collects security logs and raises alerts on suspicious activity. Its alerts can be fed in as security incidents.
The tool used to log and track IT requests, incidents and changes, such as Jira or ServiceNow. Tickets can be collected as evidence of a control operating.
The system that records customer contacts and service requests. Grievances can be fed from it.
The finance and operations system of record. It can supply data for financial reconciliations.

agents.name: Regulatory Intelligence Agent
agents.does: Reads a regulatory document and proposes clauses and obligations for the compliance team to validate.

agents.name: Compliance Mapping Agent
agents.does: Recommends which existing controls address an obligation, or drafts a new control where there is a gap.

agents.name: Risk Assessment Agent
agents.does: Suggests likelihood, impact and control effectiveness from linked controls, tests, findings and KRIs.

agents.name: Evidence Validation Agent
agents.does: Checks evidence for completeness, relevance, validity dates and inconsistencies before a reviewer decides.

agents.name: Claims Audit Agent
agents.does: Looks across claims and exceptions for unusual patterns by delegate, hospital, override and rejection reason.

agents.name: Third-Party Risk Agent
agents.does: Summarizes a delegate, hospital or vendor's weak areas from assessments, SLAs and incidents, with follow-up actions.

agents.name: Audit Reporting Agent
agents.does: Drafts the audit report from recorded findings, and suggests root cause lines of enquiry for a finding.

kpis.name: Regulatory obligation coverage
kpis.rule: Approved, applicable obligations that have a department and an owner, divided by all approved, applicable obligations.

kpis.name: Control coverage
kpis.rule: Approved, applicable obligations with at least one mapped control, divided by all approved, applicable obligations.

kpis.name: Evidence completeness
kpis.rule: Active controls with at least one accepted, unexpired evidence record, divided by all active controls.

kpis.name: Control test pass rate
kpis.rule: Active controls whose latest test passed (with or without exceptions), divided by active controls that have been tested. Untested controls are excluded.

kpis.name: Audit closure on time
kpis.rule: Findings closed on or before their due date, divided by findings that are closed or past due. Open findings not yet due are excluded.

kpis.name: Claims within timelines
kpis.rule: Evaluated claims with no open or confirmed exception (documented extensions count as within), divided by evaluated claims. Claims still inside their limits are excluded.

kpis.name: Delegate assessments in date
kpis.rule: Active delegates with an assessment that is not past its reassessment date, divided by active delegates.

kpis.name: CAPA effectiveness
kpis.rule: Corrective actions verified as effective, divided by actions whose effectiveness has been assessed.

kpis.name: Mandatory training completion
kpis.rule: Mandatory training assignments completed, divided by those completed or past their due date. Assignments not yet due are excluded.

kpis.name: Risk reduction
kpis.rule: Total inherent score minus total residual score, divided by total inherent score, across open risks that have been scored.

charts.title: Corrective actions

charts.title: Claims

charts.title: Control tests
charts.note: Tests performed, and how many of them passed.

indicators.title: Open findings backlog
indicators.basis: Findings raised minus findings closed, month by month. The dotted point is a straight-line projection for the current month from the six before it, not a forecast of certainty.

indicators.title: Claims with an exception
indicators.basis: Share of the claims registered in each month that have at least one exception. The dotted point is a straight-line projection for the current month from the six before it, not a forecast of certainty.

indicators.title: Grievances received
indicators.basis: Complaints received each month. The dotted point is a straight-line projection for the current month from the six before it, not a forecast of certainty.

indicators.title: Grievance resolution gap
indicators.basis: Complaints received minus complaints resolved in the same month. The dotted point is a straight-line projection for the current month from the six before it, not a forecast of certainty.

indicators.title: Control test failure rate
indicators.basis: Tests that failed as a share of tests performed in the month. The dotted point is a straight-line projection for the current month from the six before it, not a forecast of certainty.

kpis.name: Control coverage
kpis.rule: Approved, applicable obligations with at least one mapped control, divided by all approved, applicable obligations.

kpis.name: Evidence completeness
kpis.rule: Active controls with at least one accepted, unexpired evidence record, divided by all active controls.

kpis.name: Control test pass rate
kpis.rule: Active controls whose latest test passed (with or without exceptions), divided by active controls that have been tested. Untested controls are excluded.

kpis.name: Audit closure on time
kpis.rule: Findings closed on or before their due date, divided by findings that are closed or past due. Open findings not yet due are excluded.

kpis.name: Claims within timelines
kpis.rule: Evaluated claims with no open or confirmed exception (documented extensions count as within), divided by evaluated claims. Claims still inside their limits are excluded.

kpis.name: Delegate assessments in date
kpis.rule: Active delegates with an assessment that is not past its reassessment date, divided by active delegates.

kpis.name: CAPA effectiveness
kpis.rule: Corrective actions verified as effective, divided by actions whose effectiveness has been assessed.

kpis.name: Mandatory training completion
kpis.rule: Mandatory training assignments completed, divided by those completed or past their due date. Assignments not yet due are excluded.

kpis.name: Risk reduction
kpis.rule: Total inherent score minus total residual score, divided by total inherent score, across open risks that have been scored.
